In Grand Forks, North Dakota, conditions were harsh enough to surpass a temperature record set in 1979, with the mercury falling to minus 37 degrees, the National Weather Service said.

The surge of cold air, snow and ice disrupted travel across the Midwest. In cities throughout the region, schools and businesses closed because of the bitter temperatures, while residents worked to clear snow from vehicles and roads.

iReport.com: How is winter weather affecting you?

In Arlington Heights, Illinois, railroad employee Matt Tesh experienced the bite of wind chills near zero as he cleared snow from train tracks Tuesday morning, CNN affiliate WGN reported.

See how the storm has hit Chicago, Illinois »

Tesh, dressed in multiple layers beneath a bright orange coat, initially attempted to work without covering his face. He quickly changed his mind.

“Two or three minutes [without it], and my face was burning,” he told WGN.

Forecasters said little relief is expected over the next several days. The system, called an “Alberta clipper,” is forecast to bring strong gusts, sharply falling temperatures and a few inches of snow to Chicago, Illinois, on Wednesday morning, according to the National Weather Service.

CNN meteorologist Guillermo Arduino said the Canadian cold system will collide with another system that began in the Arctic, spreading subfreezing temperatures across the Great Lakes region.

See the forecast »

The weather pattern is expected to give many Midwestern states their coldest days of the season, along with dangerous wind chills. National Weather Service forecasters said 1 to 5 inches of snow could fall from the Dakotas through the southern Great Lakes and into the Northeast by week’s end.

“Near-whiteout conditions and slick roads are expected to impact travel of all types,” the weather service’s central region headquarters said.

Arduino said airports in Chicago; Minneapolis; Milwaukee, Wisconsin; and Grand Rapids and Detroit, Michigan, are likely to continue seeing delays following earlier waves of snow and cold.

Detroit temperatures are forecast to fall to minus 18 degrees Wednesday and minus 12 degrees Thursday. In Minneapolis, the front is expected to drive readings down to minus 21 degrees Wednesday and minus 29 degrees Thursday.

In Bismarck, North Dakota, Wednesday temperatures are expected to drop close to minus 20, with wind chills possibly reaching as low as minus 45 degrees. Forecasters said the city could get another 3 to 6 inches of snow over the next couple of days, adding to the 5 inches left behind by the previous winter storm.

# Blizzard conditions and dangerous cold grip the Upper Midwest and Great Lakes

A powerful cold front sweeping across the Upper Midwest and Great Lakes is bringing blizzard conditions, plunging temperatures and hazardous travel to millions of people, with officials warning residents to stay off roads as blowing snow and ice create whiteout conditions.

The storm system, fueled by Arctic air surging south out of Canada, is producing heavy snow, wind gusts strong enough to knock out power and wind chills that could become life-threatening in parts of Minnesota, Wisconsin, North Dakota, Illinois and Michigan.

Forecasters warned that conditions could deteriorate quickly through the day as temperatures fall sharply behind the front. In some areas, rain is expected to flash-freeze on roads before changing to snow, increasing the risk of crashes and stranded drivers.

## Minnesota sees whiteouts and road closures

In Minnesota, blizzard warnings covered large portions of the state, including areas west and north of the Twin Cities, where strong winds were whipping freshly fallen snow across highways and rural roads.

Transportation officials reported rapidly worsening visibility on interstates and secondary roads, with some stretches becoming nearly impassable. Plow crews were working in difficult conditions, but officials cautioned that drifting snow could cover treated roads within minutes.

Schools in several districts shifted to remote learning or canceled classes, while emergency managers urged residents to delay travel and prepare for possible power outages. In the Twin Cities, commuters faced slick roads, flight delays and bitter wind chills as the cold front pushed through.

## Wisconsin faces snow, ice and lakeshore winds

Across Wisconsin, heavy snow and gusty winds created dangerous travel from the western part of the state to the Lake Michigan shoreline. Areas around Madison, Green Bay and Milwaukee were expected to see a mix of snow, blowing snow and rapidly falling temperatures.

Along the lakeshore, winds off Lake Michigan intensified the storm’s impact, reducing visibility and raising concerns about icy roads and localized power outages. Officials said bridges, overpasses and untreated roads could become especially dangerous as temperatures dropped below freezing.

Emergency crews urged drivers to keep blankets, phone chargers, water and emergency supplies in their vehicles if travel was unavoidable.

## North Dakota hit by extreme cold and drifting snow

North Dakota was among the hardest-hit areas as the Arctic front brought intense cold, strong winds and widespread blowing snow.

Communities across the state reported near-whiteout conditions at times, particularly in open rural areas where there are few natural windbreaks. Wind chills were expected to fall to dangerous levels, increasing the risk of frostbite in as little as minutes for anyone exposed without proper winter clothing.

State officials warned that stranded motorists could face life-threatening conditions and urged residents to avoid unnecessary travel until winds diminish and crews can clear roads.

## Illinois braces for freezing roads and bitter wind

In Illinois, the cold front brought a sharp change in conditions, with rain, sleet or wet roads in some areas expected to freeze as temperatures plunged. Northern Illinois, including the Chicago area, faced snow squalls, strong winds and deteriorating travel conditions.

Air travelers at Chicago’s airports were advised to check flight status as delays and cancellations mounted due to snow, wind and deicing operations. Road crews treated major routes, but officials said rapidly falling temperatures could make salt less effective and allow ice to form quickly.

Chicago officials also urged residents to check on vulnerable neighbors and use warming centers as wind chills dropped.

## Michigan faces lake-effect snow and hazardous travel

Michigan was expected to see some of the most persistent snowfall as cold air moved over the Great Lakes, triggering lake-effect snow bands.

Western and northern Michigan faced the highest snow totals, with communities near Lake Michigan at risk of heavy bursts of snow and sudden drops in visibility. The Upper Peninsula also faced dangerous wind chills, drifting snow and difficult travel conditions.

Forecasters warned that lake-effect bands could vary dramatically over short distances, with one town seeing only light snow while another nearby experiences several inches in a short period.

## Officials warn of life-threatening cold

The biggest danger behind the storm may be the cold. Arctic air pouring into the region is expected to send wind chills well below zero across much of the Upper Midwest and Great Lakes.

Health officials warned that frostbite and hypothermia can develop quickly in these conditions. Residents were urged to limit time outdoors, dress in layers, cover exposed skin and bring pets inside.

Emergency management agencies also encouraged residents to prepare for power outages by charging phones, checking batteries, keeping generators outdoors and away from windows, and ensuring heating systems are safely operating.

Forecasters said conditions may remain hazardous even after snowfall ends, as strong winds continue to blow snow across roads and dangerously cold temperatures linger into the coming days.

A powerful winter storm that dumped heavy snow across parts of the northern United States has been followed by a brutal blast of Arctic air, leaving millions facing dangerous wind chills, widespread travel disruptions and life-threatening conditions.
